message: O que é RAG e como funciona a recuperação?
answer:
RAG, ou Retrieval-Augmented Generation, é um padrão que combina um modelo de linguagem com recuperação de informações externas para melhorar a qualidade das respostas. Em vez de depender apenas do que o modelo aprendeu durante o treinamento, o sistema busca documentos relevantes no momento da consulta e os inclui no contexto do prompt. Isso ajuda a reduzir alucinações e permite responder perguntas sobre dados privados ou recentes que o modelo não viu antes.

O funcionamento da recuperação em RAG ocorre em duas fases principais:

1. Fase offline de ingestão: os documentos fonte são carregados, divididos em pedaços (chunks), e para cada pedaço é calculado um vetor de embedding, que é armazenado em um banco de dados vetorial.

2. Fase online de recuperação: a consulta do usuário é transformada em embedding pelo mesmo modelo, e é feita uma busca por vizinhos mais próximos para encontrar os pedaços mais similares. Esses pedaços são então inseridos no prompt enviado ao modelo de linguagem para gerar a resposta.

A qualidade do sistema RAG depende muito da qualidade da recuperação, ou seja, se os pedaços corretos não forem recuperados, o modelo não conseguirá responder corretamente, independentemente do prompt. Por isso, a escolha do embedding, a estratégia de divisão dos documentos e a métrica de similaridade são fatores cruciais para a precisão do RAG.

chunks.text:
# Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a pattern that grounds a language model in
external knowledge. Instead of relying only on what the model memorized during
training, the system retrieves relevant documents at query time and places them
in the prompt as context. This reduces hallucinations and lets the model answer
questions about private or recent data it never saw during training.
chunks.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

chunks.text:
The quality of a RAG system depends on retrieval quality. If the right chunk is
never retrieved, no amount of prompting will recover the answer. This is why
embedding choice, chunking strategy, and the similarity metric are the levers
that most affect RAG accuracy.
chunks.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

chunks.text:
A typical RAG pipeline has two phases. The offline **ingestion** phase loads
source documents, splits them into chunks, computes an embedding vector for each
chunk, and stores those vectors in a vector database. The online **retrieval**
phase embeds the user's query with the same model, performs a nearest-neighbor
search to find the most similar chunks, and injects the top matches into the
prompt sent to the LLM.
chunks.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

chunks.text:
Generation is **autoregressive**: the model produces one token at a time, and
each new token is appended to the input before predicting the next. This is why
responses can be streamed — the application can display each token the moment it
is produced instead of waiting for the whole answer. It is also why longer
answers take longer: every token is a separate forward pass through the network.

[rag.md] # Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a pattern that grounds a language model in
external knowledge. Instead of relying only on what the model memorized during
training, the system retrieves relevant documents at query time and places them
in the prompt as context. This reduces hallucinations and lets the model answer
questions about private or recent data it never saw during training.

[rag.md] The quality of a RAG system depends on retrieval quality. If the right chunk is
never retrieved, no amount of prompting will recover the answer. This is why
embedding choice, chunking strategy, and the similarity metric are the levers
that most affect RAG accuracy.

[rag.md] A typical RAG pipeline has two phases. The offline **ingestion** phase loads
source documents, splits them into chunks, computes an embedding vector for each
chunk, and stores those vectors in a vector database. The online **retrieval**
phase embeds the user's query with the same model, performs a nearest-neighbor
search to find the most similar chunks, and injects the top matches into the
prompt sent to the LLM.

[llm-basics.md] Generation is **autoregressive**: the model produces one token at a time, and
each new token is appended to the input before predicting the next. This is why
responses can be streamed — the application can display each token the moment it
is produced instead of waiting for the whole answer. It is also why longer
answers take longer: every token is a separate forward pass through the network.
